papers.title: Hole-doping induced ferromagnetism in 2D materials
papers.authors: Ruishen Meng, Lino da Costa Pereira, Jean-Pierre Locquet, Valeri Afanas’ev, Geoffrey Pourtois
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic materials are considered as promising candidates for the future generations of spintronic devices. Yet, 2D materials with intrinsic ferromagnetism are scarce. Hereby, high-throughput first-principles simulations are performed to screen 2D materials that present a non-magnetic to a ferromagnetic transition upon hole doping. A global evolutionary search is subsequently performed to identify alternative possible atomic structures of the eligible candidates, and 122 materials exhibiting a hole-doping induced ferromagnetism are identified. Their energetic and dynamic stability, as well as magnetic properties under hole doping are investigated systematically. Half of these 2D materials are metal halides, followed by chalcogenides, oxides, and nitrides, some of them having predicted Curie temperatures above 300 K. The exchange interactions responsible for the ferromagnetic order are also discussed. This work not only provides theoretical insights into hole-doped 2D ferromagnetic materials, but also enriches the family of 2D magnetic materials for possible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Antisite defect qubits in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.
papers.notes: Good reference for antisite defects in TMDs.

papers.title: Universal hydrogen-free synthesis and elemental doping of two-dimensional transition metal selenides
papers.authors: Ping Man, Lok Wing Wong, Ka Ho Leung, Zhiqiang Guan, Tianren Chen, Honglin Chen et al.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal selenides (TMSs) feature notable bandgap flexibility, versatile doping characteristics, and practical manufacturability, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation electronics. However, their synthesis remains a critical bottleneck, as conventional chemical vapor deposition (CVD) routes require H2 assistance for selenization, raising safety, cost, and quality concerns and constraining elemental doping. Here we show a universal, H2-free CVD method that overcomes these limitations. Our approach produces a broad spectrum of 2D TMSs, including monolayer binaries, bilayer polytypes, alloys, and heterostructures, and is compatible with diverse substrates. Incorporating common metals (Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Cu) into the precursor enhances growth kinetics and enables precise doping. Al-doped WSe2 exhibits markedly lower resistance, with centimeter-scale films attaining a hole mobility of 28.36 cm2 V−1 s−1 and an on/off ratio of 3.56×106, comparable to exfoliated and H2-assisted monolayers. This work establishes a safe, scalable, and tunable synthesis strategy for high-performance 2D electronics. 2D transition metal selenides (TMSs) exhibit interesting (opto-)electronic properties, but their bottom-up synthesis usually requires H2 gas, leading to safety concerns and cost implications. Here, the authors report a universal H2-free chemical vapour deposition method to grow large-scale metal-doped 2D TMSs on various substrates.

papers.title: What Is the Role of a Magnetic Mo Antisite Defect on Carrier Relaxation and Spin Dynamics in 2-D MoS<sub>2</sub>?
papers.authors: Chengan Lei, Zhao Qian, Yandong Ma, Rajeev Ahuja
papers.abstract: Antisite defects significantly influence the dynamic properties of monolayer MoS 2, yet the carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in spin-polarized Mo antisite-defective MoS 2 remain unclear. Understanding these processes is crucial for advancing optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices. Here, we employ first-principles calculations and ab initio nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with spin–orbit coupling (SOC) to explore carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with a Mo antisite defect. This defect alters the material’s magnetic properties, leading to distinct relaxation behaviors: electron relaxation is slower than hole relaxation, and charge carriers in different spin channels exhibit varied dynamics. These differences arise from variations in electron–phonon coupling, SOC strength, and phonon mode activation. Our findings provide key insights into charge and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with magnetic defects and suggest strategies to enhance the performance of next-generation optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices.

news_articles.title: High-Throughput DFT Screening of 2D Transition Metal Carbonitrides for Solid-State Battery Solid Electrolyte Interphases
news_articles.affiliations: ¹ School of Advanced Materials Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea
news_articles.keywords: Solid-State Batteries, MXenes, DFT, High-Throughput Screening, VASP, LLZO
news_articles.abstract: The interface stability between garnet-type solid electrolytes (e.g., Li7La3Zr2O12, LLZO) and lithium metal anodes remains the primary bottleneck for next-generation solid-state batteries. We report a comprehensive high-throughput computational screening over 45 functionalized 2D transition metal carbonitrides (MXenes and MAB phases). By computing grand potential phase diagrams and interfacial reaction energies, we identify Ti3C2F2 and V2CTx as superior artificial SEI interlayers that effectively suppress lithium dendrite nucleation.
news_articles.content_html:
1. Background & Motivation

All-solid-state lithium metal batteries promise game-changing energy densities exceeding 500 Wh/kg. However, severe chemical side-reactions and dendrite propagation across the garnet electrolyte/lithium metal interface critically shorten cycle lifetime. In this study, we screen 2D transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) to design an ultra-thin, chemo-mechanically robust artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).

2. High-Throughput Computational Workflow

A Python-automated high-throughput DFT pipeline utilizing VASP and pymatgen screened 45 surface-terminated MXene compositions (M2X, M3X2, M4X3; M = Ti, V, Nb, Mo; Tx = O, F, OH, Cl). Li-ion diffusion pathways across the interfacial grain boundaries were evaluated using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method with 7 intermediate images.

ΔEinterface = Ebilayer - EMXene - ELLZO(001)
(1)

3. Interfacial Stability & Lithium Diffusion Barriers

Among all candidates, fluorinated titanium carbide Ti3C2F2 demonstrated an ideal balance of low Li-ion migration barrier (0.22 eV) and thermodynamic passivity against metallic lithium reduction. The computed grand-potential phase diagram indicates complete electrochemical stability from 0.0 V to 2.4 V vs Li/Li+.

4. Summary & Outlook

Our findings establish atomic-level design guidelines for stabilizing solid-state lithium battery interfaces, paving the way for targeted experimental synthesis in the upcoming quarter.

In addition, our lab has signed a formal collaborative computing and experimental synthesis agreement with KIST Center for Computational Materials Science.
news_articles.content_html:
1. High-Performance Computing Cluster Expansion

To support high-throughput DFT simulations and hybrid functional calculations of large defect supercells, our research group has completed the deployment and commissioning of the SKKU-CMS-Node03 computing cluster. Specifications:

  • CPUs: Dual AMD EPYC 9554 processors (128 physical cores, 256 threads @ up to 3.75 GHz)

  • Software Stack: VASP 6.4.2 compiled with OpenMPI 4.1.6, Intel oneMKL, and CUDA OpenACC GPU offloading

2. Benchmark Results on 2D Supercells

Benchmarking on a 216-atom 2D MoSi2N4 defect supercell with HSE06 hybrid functional demonstrated a 4.2× walltime reduction compared to our previous dual Xeon Gold nodes. Self-consistent electronic convergence was achieved within 38 minutes per k-point configuration.

3. Collaboration with KIST

Furthermore, under the new MoU with the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST), our group will gain access to shared supercomputing allocations on the KIST K-CREST infrastructure to perform ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations of molten salt synthesis.

dft_lectures.title: Lecture 1: Quantum Many-Body Problem, Hohenberg–Kohn Theorems & Kohn–Sham DFT
dft_lectures.subtitle: From the exact 3N-dimensional Schrödinger equation and Levy–Lieb constrained search to the self-consistent Kohn–Sham orbital formalism and Pulay/Kerker SCF mixing.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: schrodinger born oppenheimer many-body hohenberg kohn levy lieb variational kohn-sham janak scf self-consistent field pulay kerker hartree density functional convergence
objectives: Explain why solving the interacting many-electron Schrödinger equation directly is exponentially intractable and derive the Born–Oppenheimer separation.
Master the Hohenberg–Kohn theorems and Levy–Lieb constrained search establishing electron density n(r) as the exact ground-state variable.
Derive the Kohn–Sham single-particle equations, Janak's theorem, and the physical distinction between KS eigenvalues and quasiparticle energies.
Trace the Self-Consistent Field (SCF) loop including Pulay DIIS density mixing and Kerker preconditioning against charge sloshing.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
1.1 The Many-Body Problem & Born–Oppenheimer Approximation

Every equilibrium and dynamical property of a crystal, surface, or molecule—its lattice constants, electronic band gap, magnetism, optical spectrum, and catalytic activity—is governed by the non-relativistic time-independent many-body Schrödinger equation for N electrons at coordinates {ri} and M nuclei of charges ZI and masses MI at positions {RI}:

\hat{H}\,\Psi\!\left(\{\mathbf{r}_i\}, \{\mathbf{R}_I\}\right) = E\,\Psi\!\left(\{\mathbf{r}_i\}, \{\mathbf{R}_I\}\right)
(1.1)

In atomic units (ℏ = me = e = 4πε0 = 1, where lengths are in Bohr a0 = 0.529177 Å and energies in Hartree 1 Ha = 27.211386 eV), the exact molecular or crystalline Hamiltonian comprises five distinct physical operators:

\hat{H} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_i^2 - \sum_{I=1}^{M}\frac{1}{2M_I}\nabla_I^2 - \sum_{i,I}\frac{Z_I}{\left|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}_I\right|} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\right|} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{I\neq J}\frac{Z_I Z_J}{\left|\mathbf{R}_I - \mathbf{R}_J\right|}
(1.2)
Terms left to right: electronic kinetic energy Te, nuclear kinetic energy Tn, electron–nucleus Coulomb attraction Vne, electron–electron Coulomb repulsion Vee, and nucleus–nucleus Ewald repulsion EII.
📘 Definition — Born–Oppenheimer (Adiabatic) Approximation
Because nuclei are 1,836 to >400,000 times heavier than electrons (MI ≫ me), electrons relax almost instantaneously to any nuclear displacement. Factoring the wavefunction as Ψ({ri}, {RI}) ≈ ψel({ri}; {RI}) χnuc({RI}) decouples nuclear motion and solves the electronic problem at fixed nuclear positions {RI}. The parametric electronic ground-state energy plus EII defines the Potential Energy Surface (PES) E({RI}).

Under the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, the clamped nuclei produce a static external potential vext(r) = −∑I ZI / |r − RI|, reducing Eq. (1.2) to the interacting electronic Hamiltonian:

\hat{H}_{\mathrm{el}} = \hat{T}_{\mathrm{e}} + \hat{V}_{\mathrm{ee}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}_i)
(1.3)

Why Wavefunction Methods Hit an Exponential Wall: Representing the antisymmetric wavefunction ψ(r1, …, rN) on a coarse 10-point 3D grid per electron requires 103N complex amplitudes. Even for a single Fe atom (N = 26), 1078 numbers exceeds the count of atoms in the observable universe. Density Functional Theory bypasses this exponential barrier completely.

1.2 Electron Density, Hohenberg–Kohn Theorems & Levy–Lieb Search

Instead of the 3N-dimensional wavefunction, DFT uses the 3-dimensional electron number density n(r)—a scalar physical observable depending on only three spatial coordinates (x, y, z):

n(\mathbf{r}) = N \int \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}_2 \cdots \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}_N \allowbreak\,\left|\psi(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N)\right|^2, \qquad \int n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} = N
(1.4)
📘 Definition — Hohenberg–Kohn Theorem I (Uniqueness)
For any system of interacting electrons in a non-degenerate ground state, the ground-state density n0(r) uniquely determines the external potential vext(r) up to a trivial additive constant. Hence n0(r) uniquely determines the entire Hamiltonian, ψ0[n0], and every ground-state physical observable as a functional of n(r).
📘 Definition — Hohenberg–Kohn Theorem II (Variational Principle)
A universal functional FHK[n] independent of vext(r) exists such that E[n] = FHK[n] + ∫vext(r)n(r)d3r attains its exact global minimum E0 if and only if n(r) = n0(r): E[n] ≥ E[n0] = E0.

To eliminate the original v-representability restriction of Hohenberg and Kohn (1964) and cover degenerate ground states, Mel Levy (1979) and Elliott Lieb (1983) formulated the rigorous Constrained-Search Functional minimizing over all antisymmetric N-electron wavefunctions yielding a given density n(r):

F_{\mathrm{LL}}[n] = \min_{\psi \to n}\langle \psi | \hat{T}_{\mathrm{e}} + \hat{V}_{\mathrm{ee}} | \psi \rangle, \qquad E_0 = \min_{n}\left\{\, F_{\mathrm{LL}}[n] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} \,\right\}
(1.5)

1.3 The Kohn–Sham Ansatz (1965) & Janak's Theorem

Although FLL[n] is formally exact, direct density-only kinetic energy functionals (such as Thomas–Fermi) fail to reproduce atomic shell structure or chemical bonding. Walter Kohn and Lu Jeu Sham solved this by mapping the interacting system onto a fictitious system of N non-interacting electrons moving in an effective local potential veff(r) whose ground-state density equals the exact interacting density:

n(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i\,\left|\phi_i(\mathbf{r})\right|^2
(1.6)
where φi(r) are orthonormal Kohn–Sham orbitals and fi ∈ [0, 2] (or [0, 1] per spin channel) are occupation numbers.

The Kohn–Sham total energy functional separates four explicitly computable pieces from a single remaining unknown term, the exchange–correlation functional Exc[n]:

E_{\mathrm{KS}}[n] = T_{\mathrm{s}}\!\left[\{\phi_i\}\right] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} + E_{\mathrm{H}}[n] + E_{\mathrm{xc}}[n] + E_{\mathrm{II}}
(1.7)
T_{\mathrm{s}}\!\left[\{\phi_i\}\right] = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i \int \phi_i^*(\mathbf{r})\,\nabla^2\phi_i(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}}[n] = \frac{1}{2}\iint \frac{n(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r}')}{\left|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'\right|}\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}'
(1.8)

Imposing stationarity δEKS / δφi* = 0 with Lagrange multipliers ϵi enforcing orthonormality ⟨φi|φj⟩ = δij yields the Kohn–Sham single-particle equations:

\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0}\nabla^2 + v_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r})\right]\phi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \varepsilon_i\,\phi_i(\mathbf{r}), \qquad v_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}) = v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}) + v_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{r}) + \frac{\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]}{\delta n(\mathbf{r})}
(1.9)
💡 Physical Insight — Physical Meaning of Kohn–Sham Eigenvalues & Janak's Theorem
Strictly speaking, Kohn–Sham eigenvalues ϵi are Lagrange multipliers of the auxiliary non-interacting system, not exact single-electron removal energies. However, Janak's Theorem proves ∂EKS/∂fi = ϵi, and for the exact functional the highest occupied eigenvalue equals the negative exact ionization potential (ϵHOMO = −I). In practice, KS eigenvalues provide an excellent starting description of band dispersion and orbital ordering, while quantitative band gaps require Hybrid DFT (HSE06) or many-body GW corrections (Lecture 2).

1.4 The Self-Consistent Field (SCF) Loop, Pulay Mixing & Kerker Damping

Because vH[n] and vxc[n] depend on the output density nout(r), Eq. (1.9) must be iterated to self-consistency. Simple linear mixing diverges in metallic slabs because the Hartree potential scales as 4π/q2 at long wavelengths (q → 0), causing charge sloshing. Modern codes (CASTEP, VASP) combine Pulay DIIS with Kerker reciprocal-space preconditioning:

G_{\mathrm{Kerker}}(q) = A\,\frac{q^2}{q^2 + q_0^2}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{in}}^{(k+1)}(\mathbf{q}) = n_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(k)}(\mathbf{q}) + G_{\mathrm{Kerker}}(q)\,R_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(k)}(\mathbf{q})
(1.10)
Kerker preconditioning damps long-wavelength q → 0 charge sloshing while accelerating short-wavelength convergence (controlled in CASTEP via mix_charge_amp and mix_charge_gmax).

dft_lectures.contentHtml:
2.1 What Lives Inside Exc[n] & Why Semilocal Band Gaps Are Too Small

Kohn–Sham DFT is formally exact—all many-body quantum mechanics beyond classical electrostatics is concentrated into a single universal functional, Exc[n]:

E_{\mathrm{xc}}[n] = \left(T_{\mathrm{e}}[n] - T_{\mathrm{s}}[n]\right) + \left(V_{\mathrm{ee}}[n] - E_{\mathrm{H}}[n]\right)
(2.1)
Exc accounts for: (1) Pauli Fermi exchange keeping parallel-spin electrons apart, (2) dynamical Coulomb correlation keeping antiparallel electrons apart, (3) exact cancellation of unphysical Hartree self-interaction, and (4) the interacting vs. non-interacting kinetic energy difference.

Even for the exact Kohn–Sham functional, the fundamental experimental band gap Eg = I − A (ionization potential minus electron affinity) exceeds the Kohn–Sham eigenvalue gap EgKS = ϵCBM − ϵVBM by the exchange–correlation derivative discontinuity Δxc as electron number crosses an integer N:

E_{\mathrm{g}}^{\mathrm{exact}} = E_{\mathrm{g}}^{\mathrm{KS}} + \Delta_{\mathrm{xc}}, \qquad \Delta_{\mathrm{xc}} = \lim_{\eta \to 0^+}\!\left[\,v_{\mathrm{xc}}^{N+\eta}(\mathbf{r}) - v_{\mathrm{xc}}^{N-\eta}(\mathbf{r})\,\right]
(2.2)
Because continuous semilocal functionals (LDA, PBE) have Δxc = 0 and suffer from delocalization (self-interaction) error, they systematically underestimate semiconductor band gaps by 30–50%.

2.2 Perdew's Jacob's Ladder of Exchange–Correlation Functionals

John Perdew organized XC approximations into five ascending rungs moving from the Hartree world toward "chemical accuracy" (1 kcal/mol ≈ 0.043 eV):

1. Local Density Approximation (LDA): Models every local volume d3r as a homogeneous electron gas parameterized from Ceperley–Alder Quantum Monte Carlo data:

E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}[n] = \int n(\mathbf{r})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{unif}}\!\left(n(\mathbf{r})\right)\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}
(2.3)

2. Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA — PBE / PBEsol / RPBE): Modulates uniform exchange via an enhancement factor Fxc(n, s) depending on the dimensionless reduced density gradient s = |∇n| / (2kFn):

E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{GGA}}[n] = \int n(\mathbf{r})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{unif}}(n)\,F_{\mathrm{xc}}(n, s)\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}
(2.4)

3. Meta-GGA (SCAN / r2SCAN): Introduces the Kohn–Sham orbital kinetic energy density τ(r) = ½∑i|∇φi|2 through the dimensionless iso-orbital indicator α(r) that automatically recognizes bonding regimes:

\alpha(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\tau(\mathbf{r}) - \tau^{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{r})}{\tau^{\mathrm{unif}}(\mathbf{r})}, \qquad \tau^{\mathrm{W}} = \frac{|\nabla n|^2}{8n}, \qquad \tau^{\mathrm{unif}} = \frac{3}{10}(3\pi^2)^{2/3}\,n^{5/3}
(2.5)
α = 0 flags single-orbital covalent regions, α ≈ 1 flags metallic uniform regions, and α ≫ 1 flags weak non-covalent / van der Waals overlap—allowing SCAN to satisfy all 17 known exact semilocal constraints.

4. Screened Range-Separated Hybrid Functional (HSE06): Splits the Coulomb interaction 1/r = erfc(ωr)/r + erf(ωr)/r (ω = 0.2 Å−1) and mixes 25% exact short-range Hartree–Fock exchange, restoring non-zero generalized KS derivative discontinuity and experimental-grade semiconductor band gaps:

E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{HSE06}} = \frac{1}{4}E_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{HF,SR}}(\omega) + \frac{3}{4}E_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{PBE,SR}}(\omega) + E_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{PBE,LR}}(\omega) + E_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{PBE}}
(2.6)

2.3 Long-Range van der Waals Dispersion Corrections (DFT-D2/D3 & TS)

Standard LDA and GGA functionals decay exponentially where electron clouds do not overlap and therefore completely omit long-range London dispersion (−C6/R6) from correlated quantum dipole fluctuations. Without dispersion corrections, graphite, 2D heterobilayers (MoS2/WS2), and physisorbed molecules fail to bind at the correct interlayer distance! Pairwise DFT-D adds a damped asymptotic tail:

E_{\mathrm{DFT\text{-}D}} = E_{\mathrm{KS\text{-}DFT}} - s_6 \sum_{I < J}\frac{C_6^{IJ}}{R_{IJ}^6}\,f_{\mathrm{damp}}(R_{IJ})
(2.7)
In CASTEP, sedc_scheme: G06 activates Grimme DFT-D2 (fixed atomic C6), TS activates Tkatchenko–Scheffler (environment-dependent Hirshfeld-volume-scaled C6eff and polarizabilities), and MBD* captures full many-body collective screening.

2.4 Strongly Correlated 3d/4f Systems: Dudarev DFT+U

For transition-metal oxides, Prussian Blue analogues (e.g. KCoHCF), and lanthanides with tightly localized 3d or 4f shells, GGA overly delocalizes electrons and can falsely predict magnetic insulators to be non-magnetic metals. The rotationally invariant Dudarev DFT+U penalty discourages fractional orbital occupations nmσ ∈ (0, 1) and restores integer orbital occupancy and Mott/charge-transfer gaps:

E_{\mathrm{DFT}+U} = E_{\mathrm{DFT}} + \frac{U_{\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\sum_{I,\sigma}\sum_{m} n_{m\sigma}^I\left(1 - n_{m\sigma}^I\right), \qquad U_{\mathrm{eff}} = U - J
(2.8)
Crucially, total energies computed with different Ueff values cannot be subtracted directly; keep Ueff identical (or justify via linear-response Cococcioni–de Gironcoli theory) when comparing polymorphs or redox phases.

dft_lectures.title: Lecture 3: Periodic Crystals, Bloch's Theorem, Plane Waves, Pseudopotentials & k-Sampling
dft_lectures.subtitle: How periodic boundary conditions reduce an infinite Avogadro-scale crystal to one unit cell, a plane-wave cutoff Ecut, PAW/USPP pseudopotentials, and an irreducible k-point grid.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: crystal lattice bravais reciprocal brillouin zone bloch theorem plane wave cutoff ecut pseudopotential ncpp uspp paw otfg monkhorst pack kpoint smearing methfessel paxton slab vacuum miller index
objectives: Relate real-space Bravais lattice vectors A to reciprocal-space vectors B and the First Brillouin Zone.
Apply Bloch's theorem to expand crystal wavefunctions in a finite plane-wave basis set truncated systematically by Ecut.
Understand Norm-Conserving (NCPP), Ultrasoft (USPP/OTFG), and Projector Augmented Wave (PAW) all-electron reconstruction.
Design converged Monkhorst–Pack k-point meshes, metallic smearing with T → 0 extrapolation, and 2D slabs with vacuum.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
3.1 Real-Space & Reciprocal-Space Lattices

An ideal crystal repeats a finite unit cell defined by three lattice vectors a1, a2, a3 (volume Ω = |a1 · (a2 × a3)|). Every atom's Cartesian position is r = f1a1 + f2a2 + f3a3 in fractional coordinates (f1, f2, f3) ∈ [0, 1). The dual reciprocal lattice vectors b1, b2, b3 (units: Å−1) satisfy bi · aj = 2πδij:

\mathbf{b}_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega}(\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3), \qquad \mathbf{b}_2 = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega}(\mathbf{a}_3 \times \mathbf{a}_1), \qquad \mathbf{b}_3 = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega}(\mathbf{a}_1 \times \mathbf{a}_2)
(3.1)

The Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice is the First Brillouin Zone (BZ), enclosing every inequivalent crystal wavevector k.

3.2 Bloch's Theorem & Plane-Wave Basis Expansion

📘 Definition — Bloch's Theorem (1929)
In any periodic potential veff(r + R) = veff(r), every Kohn–Sham eigenstate takes the form of a plane wave modulated by a cell-periodic function unk(r + R) = unk(r), indexed by band number n and wavevector k inside the First Brillouin Zone.

Expanding unk}(r) as a Fourier series over reciprocal lattice vectors G = m1b1 + m2b2 + m3b3 yields the universal plane-wave basis set of CASTEP, VASP, and Quantum ESPRESSO:

\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) = e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,u_{n\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\Omega}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}} c_{n,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}}\,e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}
(3.2)

The infinite Fourier expansion is truncated cleanly by one systematic convergence knob—the plane-wave kinetic energy cutoff Ecut (eV):

\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0}\left|\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{G}\right|^2 \le E_{\mathrm{cut}}
(3.3)
Increasing Ecut monotonically refines spatial resolution everywhere in space uniformly—guaranteeing zero Pulay basis-derivative forces and zero Basis Set Superposition Error (BSSE).

3.3 Pseudopotentials (NCPP, USPP) & Projector Augmented Wave (PAW)

Close to an atomic nucleus (r < rc), valence wavefunctions oscillate rapidly to remain orthogonal to tightly bound core shells (1s, 2s, 2p, …), which would require prohibitive Ecut (>105 eV). Pseudopotentials freeze the chemically inert core and replace the −Z/r Coulomb singularity and nodal valence states inside cutoff radius rc with a smooth, nodeless pseudo-wavefunction ψPS(r) matching the exact all-electron ψAE(r) identically for r ≥ rc. Blöchl's PAW formalism further reconstructs the exact all-electron wavefunction via a linear transformation:

\left|\psi_n^{\mathrm{AE}}\right\rangle = \left|\tilde{\psi}_n\right\rangle + \sum_{i}\left(\left|\phi_i^{\mathrm{AE}}\right\rangle - \left|\tilde{\phi}_i\right\rangle\right)\left\langle \tilde{p}_i \middle| \tilde{\psi}_n \right\rangle
(3.4)
PAW retains full core-region accuracy (essential for NMR, hyperfine fields, and 3d/4f magnetism) while keeping the low plane-wave cutoff of Ultrasoft pseudopotentials.

3.4 Brillouin-Zone Sampling, Metallic Smearing & 2D Supercell Vacuum

Integrals over the First Brillouin Zone are discretized on a uniform Monkhorst–Pack k-mesh (N1 × N2 × N3) folded by crystal symmetry into the Irreducible Brillouin Zone (IBZ) with weights wk (∑wk = 1):

\frac{1}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}}\int_{\mathrm{BZ}} g(\mathbf{k})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{k} \approx \sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathrm{IBZ}} w_{\mathbf{k}}\,g(\mathbf{k})
(3.5)
Choose k-spacing Δk ≤ 0.03 Å−1 for semiconductors (Ni ≈ |bi| / 2πΔk) and ≤ 0.02 Å−1 for metals, with N3 = 1 along the vacuum axis of a 2D slab (vacuum ≥ 15–20 Å).

In metals, the discontinuous Fermi-surface step function Θ(EF − E) converges slowly with k-points. Broadening occupations with a smearing width σ (Gaussian, Methfessel–Paxton, or Cold Smearing) introduces a fictitious electronic entropy term −TS; always report the 0 K extrapolated energy (Final energy, E-TS/2 in CASTEP / energy(sigma->0) in VASP):

F(T) = E(T) - TS, \qquad E(T \to 0) = \frac{1}{2}\big[E(T) + F(T)\big] = E(T) - \frac{1}{2}TS
(3.6)
Keep |TS| < 1 meV/atom so smearing does not distort equilibrium geometries or magnetic moments.

🧪 Build Unit Cells, Cut (hkl) Surface Slabs & Inspect Symmetry

  2. Upload any .cif or .cell file to verify exact VESTA space group, lattice vectors (a, b, c, α, β, γ), and boundary modes (Complete vs In-Cell).
  3. Create supercells (e.g., 2×2×1), cleave Miller-index surfaces (001) / (110) / (111), add a 20 Å vacuum layer, and export directly to .cell, .cif, .xsd, or VASP POSCAR.

dft_lectures.subtitle: How DFT relaxes atomic positions and lattice parameters to mechanical equilibrium, verifies dynamical phonon stability, and predicts electrocatalytic Gibbs free energy pathways.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: hellmann feynman force stress tensor pulay geometry optimization bfgs lbfgs tpsd formation energy cohesive surface energy adsorption gibbs free energy zpe phonon dynamical matrix neb activation barrier che
objectives: Derive atomic forces from the Hellmann–Feynman theorem and understand why plane waves eliminate Pulay force artifacts.
Define the Cauchy stress tensor, finite-basis Pulay stress correction, and BFGS / LBFGS relaxation criteria.
Verify dynamical stability via the harmonic phonon dynamical matrix and reaction barriers via Climbing-Image NEB.
Compute formation, surface, and adsorption Gibbs free energies using the Computational Hydrogen Electrode (CHE).
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
4.1 The Hellmann–Feynman Force Theorem

Locating the equilibrium crystal structure requires the force FI = −∂E/∂RI acting on every nucleus I. Differentiating E = ⟨Ψ|H|Ψ⟩ appears to involve costly wavefunction derivatives ∂Ψ/∂RI. Remarkably, for any normalized eigenstate ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩ = 1, those terms cancel identically:

\mathbf{F}_I = -\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{R}_I} = -\left\langle \Psi \left|\frac{\partial \hat{H}}{\partial \mathbf{R}_I}\right| \Psi \right\rangle \allowbreak = -\int n(\mathbf{r})\,\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})}{\partial \mathbf{R}_I}\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} - \frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{II}}}{\partial \mathbf{R}_I}
(4.1)
Because plane waves ei(k+G)·r do not depend on atomic coordinates RI, there are zero Pulay basis-derivative forces once SCF is tightly converged.

4.2 Stress Tensor & Variable-Cell Relaxation

When relaxing both atomic coordinates and lattice vectors (fix_all_cell: false), the macroscopic Cauchy stress tensor σαβ is the energy derivative with respect to homogeneous strain ϵαβ (1 eV/Å3 = 160.21766 GPa):

\sigma_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{1}{\Omega}\frac{\partial E}{\partial \varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}}, \qquad H = E + P\Omega
(4.2)
Under external hydrostatic pressure P, cell optimization minimizes the enthalpy H = E + PΩ. CASTEP applies an automatic finite-basis-set correction (finite_basis_corr: 2) to cancel Pulay stress caused by discrete jumps in the plane-wave count as Ω changes.

4.3 Quasi-Newton Optimization (BFGS / LBFGS) & Dynamical Phonon Stability

Near a local minimum of the Potential Energy Surface, quasi-Newton optimizers (BFGS / memory-efficient LBFGS) build an iterative inverse Hessian H−1 from successive force vectors gk = −Fk and advance along pk = −Hk−1gk until all four tolerances hold simultaneously:

Maximum ionic displacement max |ΔRI|geom_disp_tol1.0×10−3 Å5.0×10−4 Å
Maximum stress component max |σαβ|geom_stress_tol0.05 GPa≤ 0.02 GPa

Zero forces confirm a stationary point, not yet a true minimum. To prove dynamical stability, one diagonalizes the mass-weighted harmonic phonon dynamical matrix D(q) constructed from second-order force constants ΦIα,Jβ = ∂2E / (∂uIα∂uJβ) via DFPT or finite supercell displacements:

D_{I\alpha,J\beta}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{M_I M_J}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}} \Phi_{I\alpha,J\beta}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R})\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}, \qquad \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\,\mathbf{e}_\nu = \omega_\nu^2(\mathbf{q})\,\mathbf{e}_\nu
(4.3)
All real frequencies (ων2 ≥ 0 throughout the BZ) confirm dynamical stability; imaginary modes (ω2 < 0, plotted negative) signal a spontaneous structural distortion or phase instability.

4.4 Thermodynamic Stability, NEB Barriers & Computational Hydrogen Electrode

Because absolute DFT energies depend on pseudopotential cores, every physical observable is evaluated as an energy difference using identical Ecut, functional, and k-density:

E_{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{tot}}}\left[E_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathrm{A}_x\mathrm{B}_y) - x\mu_{\mathrm{A}} - y\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right], \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{surf}} = \frac{E_{\mathrm{slab}} - N_{\mathrm{slab}}E_{\mathrm{bulk}}}{2A_{\mathrm{surf}}}
(4.4)
Negative formation energy Ef < 0 indicates thermodynamic stability against elemental phases; γsurf (J/m2 or eV/Å2) gives the cleavage cost of a surface of area Asurf (factor 2 accounts for top and bottom slab faces).
E_{\mathrm{ads}} = E_{\mathrm{slab+ads}} - E_{\mathrm{slab}} - E_{\mathrm{ads(gas)}}, \qquad \Delta G(U) = E_{\mathrm{ads}} + \Delta E_{\mathrm{ZPE}} - T\Delta S - n e U_{\mathrm{RHE}}
(4.5)
Computational Hydrogen Electrode (CHE): At pH = 0 and U = 0 V, (H+ + e−) is in equilibrium with ½H2(g). Zero-point energy ΔEZPE = ½∑ℏωi comes from vibrational frequency calculations; kinetic migration/reaction barriers Ea = ETS − EIS are located along the minimum energy path using Climbing-Image NEB (CI-NEB).

🧪 Track Optimization Forces & Place Adsorbates on Surfaces

dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam

objectives: Interpret En(k) dispersion curves along standard high-symmetry BZ paths (Γ–M–K–Γ, Γ–X–M–Γ–R).
Distinguish direct vs. indirect band gaps, metals, Dirac semimetals, semiconductors, insulators, and half-metals via P(EF).
Define Total DOS g(E) and Atomic/Orbital-Projected DOS (PDOS) from CASTEP .pdos_bin projection weights.
Apply Hammer–Nørskov d-band center theory and PDOS overlap to diagnose covalent vs. ionic bonding.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
5.1 Electronic Band Structure En(k) & High-Symmetry BZ Paths

Solving the Kohn–Sham equation non-self-consistently at the converged density along high-symmetry lines of the First Brillouin Zone yields the electronic band structure Enσ(k) (band index n, spin σ ∈ {↑, ↓}). Energies are referenced to the Fermi level EF (metals) or the Valence Band Maximum (VBM) (semiconductors, so E − EVBM = 0 at VBM):

E_{\mathrm{g}} = \min_{\mathbf{k}} E_{\mathrm{CBM}}(\mathbf{k}) - \max_{\mathbf{k}} E_{\mathrm{VBM}}(\mathbf{k})
(5.1)
If kCBM = kVBM (e.g., K → K in monolayer MoS2 or Janus MoSi2N2P2), the gap is Direct (strong optical emission/absorption without phonon assistance). If kCBM ≠ kVBM (e.g., Si: Γ → Δ), it is Indirect.
Electronic PhaseFermi Level SignaturePhysical / Device Consequence
MetalBands cross EF; g(EF) > 0High free-carrier conductivity; finite Drude ωp
Semimetal / DiracVBM & CBM touch at discrete points (e.g. Graphene K)Linear dispersion E = ±ℏvFk; ultrahigh mobility
Semiconductor0.05 eV < Eg < 3.5 eVTunable conductivity, photovoltaics, FETs, photocatalysis
Wide-Gap InsulatorEg > 3.5 eVTransparent dielectrics, gate oxides
Half-Metal (Spin-Split)One spin channel metallic, opposite spin gapped (e.g., KCoHCF+K)100% spin polarization at EF — spintronics & spin filters

5.2 Total DOS, Projected DOS (.pdos_bin) & Spin Polarization

The Total Electronic Density of States g(E) counts electronic states per unit energy per unit cell across the Brillouin Zone. For finite k-meshes, Dirac delta functions are broadened via Gaussian smearing σ (typically 0.05–0.15 eV) or Blöchl's linear tetrahedron method:

g_\sigma(E) = \sum_{n,\mathbf{k}} g_{\mathrm{s}}\,w_{\mathbf{k}}\,\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(E - E_{n\mathbf{k}})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]
(5.2)
where gs = 2 for non-spin-polarized calculations and gs = 1 per spin channel (α ↑ positive, β ↓ mirrored negative) in collinear spin-polarized DFT.

To uncover which atoms and angular-momentum shells (s, p, d, f) compose the VBM and CBM, CASTEP projects Bloch states |ψnk}⟩ onto localized atomic pseudo-orbitals |χI,lm⟩ and saves the weights in binary *.pdos_bin files. For spin-polarized systems, the Fermi-level spin polarization P(EF) quantifies spintronic half-metallicity:

g_{I,lm}(E) = \sum_{n,\mathbf{k}} g_{\mathrm{s}}\,w_{\mathbf{k}}\left|\langle \chi_{I,lm} | \psi_{n\mathbf{k}} \rangle\right|^2 \delta(E - E_{n\mathbf{k}}), \qquad P(E_{\mathrm{F}}) = \frac{g_\uparrow(E_{\mathrm{F}}) - g_\downarrow(E_{\mathrm{F}})}{g_\uparrow(E_{\mathrm{F}}) + g_\downarrow(E_{\mathrm{F}})}
(5.3)
Crystal Lattice SystemStandard High-Symmetry Path (Setyawan–Curtarolo)Representative Materials
Hexagonal / 2D HoneycombΓ(0,0,0) → M(½,0,0) → K(⅓,⅓,0) → Γ(0,0,0)Graphene, MoS2, WS2, Janus MoSi2N2P2
Simple Cubic (cP)Γ(0,0,0) → X(0,½,0) → M(½,½,0) → Γ → R(½,½,½)Perovskites (SrTiO3), Prussian Blue (KCoHCF)
Face-Centered Cubic (cF)Γ → X(½,0,½) → W(½,¼,¾) → K(⅜,⅜,¾) → Γ → L(½,½,½)Si, GaAs, Cu, Au, MgO, rock-salt oxides
Tetragonal (tP)Γ → X(0,½,0) → M(½,½,0) → Γ → Z(0,0,½) → R(0,½,½) → A(½,½,½)Rutile TiO2, BaTiO3, layered cuprates
💡 Physical Insight — Reading Orbital Hybridization & the Hammer–Nørskov d-Band Center
Coincident PDOS peaks from two species at the exact same energy (for instance, Mo-4d and N-2p in MoSi2N4, or Co-3d and C/N-2p in KCoHCF) prove strong covalent orbital hybridization. In transition-metal catalysis, the first moment of the projected d-states—the d-band center ϵd = ∫E gd(E)dE / ∫gd(E)dE—governs adsorbate binding: shifting ϵd upward toward EF pushes antibonding states above EF, depopulating them and strengthening chemisorption.
HANDS-ON PRACTICE IN DATA ANALYSIS
🧪 Analyze Synchronized Band Structure & Exact .pdos_bin PDOS
  1. Open Data Analysis → 📈 Band & PDOS and load a calculation containing *_BandStr.bands and *_DOS.pdos_bin (e.g., KCoHCF+K or J1+4).
  2. Keep Zero: VBM / Fermi enabled so Band Structure and PDOS share the exact aligned zero-energy reference.
  3. Switch PDOS between Element + Orbital (e.g., Co-d, Fe-d, Mo-d, N-p), Orbital (s,p,d,f), and Spin Mirror (+α/−β) to inspect spin splitting and band-edge orbital character.
  4. Right-click either half of the canvas to copy Band Structure Only or PDOS Only at 400–600 DPI, or click ⚡ Analyze m*, Mobility & Drude → to continue into Lecture 6!

dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: effective mass parabolic kane non-parabolic dos effective mass conductivity mass mobility bardeen shockley takagi deformation potential frohlich polar optical brooks herring impurity matthiessen drude effective mass relaxation time plasma frequency exciton einstein diffusion
objectives: Extract directional electron and hole effective masses m*e, m*h using Parabolic and Kane Non-Parabolic band-edge fits.
Compute the DOS effective mass m*DOS both from valley degeneracy and directly via cumulative DFT DOS integration.
Calculate 2D Takagi and 3D Bardeen–Shockley mobilities, Fröhlich polar-optical & Brooks–Herring impurity scattering, Einstein diffusivity, and Wannier–Mott excitons.
Derive and evaluate Drude effective mass m*Drude(n, T), Drude relaxation time τe, τh, plasma frequency ℏωp, and optical conductivity σ(ω).
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
6.1 Semiclassical Dynamics & Band-Edge Effective Mass Tensor

Under an external electric field, a Bloch electron wavepacket centered at wavevector k propagates at group velocity vg = (1/ℏ)∇kEn(k) and responds to crystal forces with an inertia set by band curvature—the inverse effective mass tensor:

\frac{1}{m^*_{\alpha\beta}} = \frac{1}{\hbar^2}\frac{\partial^2 E_n(\mathbf{k})}{\partial k_\alpha \partial k_\beta} \allowbreak\;\implies\; \frac{m^*}{m_0} = \frac{7.61996\;\mathrm{eV}\!\cdot\!\text{Å}^2}{\partial^2 E / \partial k^2}
(6.1)
Steeply dispersing bands yield light, high-mobility carriers (small m*); flat localized bands (3d/4f states) yield heavy carriers (large m*). At the VBM, ∂2E/∂k2 < 0, giving positive hole mass m*h = −ℏ2/(∂2E/∂k2) > 0.

Away from the immediate band extremum (especially in narrow-gap semiconductors and heavily doped degenerate conductors), band coupling softens dispersion via the Kane Non-Parabolic Model:

\Delta E\left(1 + \alpha_{\mathrm{K}}\Delta E\right) = \frac{\hbar^2 q^2}{2m_0^*}, \qquad q = \left|\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{k}_0\right|
(6.2)
where m*0 is the band-edge effective mass and αK (eV−1) is the non-parabolicity parameter (pure parabolic limit: αK = 0; two-band k·p estimate: αK ≈ (1 − m*0/m0)2 / Eg).

6.2 Conductivity Mass vs. Direct DFT DOS Effective Mass (2D & 3D)

For anisotropic or multi-valley semiconductors with directional masses m*1, …, m*M and valley degeneracy gv (e.g., gv = 2 at hexagonal K/K′, gv = 6 in Si), electrical transport obeys the harmonic conductivity effective mass m*c = ((1/M)∑1/m*i)−1, whereas thermodynamic carrier density obeys the DOS effective mass m*DOS. Crucially, m*DOS can be extracted directly from the cumulative DFT state count Ncell(ΔE) without assuming single-valley parabolicity:

\textbf{2D Slab:}\;\frac{m^*_{\mathrm{DOS}}}{m_0} = \frac{2\pi(\hbar^2/m_0)}{g_{\mathrm{s}}\,S_{\mathrm{cell}}}\frac{N_{\mathrm{cell}}(\Delta E)}{\Delta E}, \qquad \textbf{3D Bulk:}\;\frac{m^*_{\mathrm{DOS}}}{m_0} = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0\Delta E}\left(\frac{6\pi^2\,N_{\mathrm{cell}}(\Delta E)}{g_{\mathrm{s}}\,\Omega}\right)^{2/3}
(6.3)

From m*DOS,e, m*DOS,h, band gap Eg, and dielectric constant ϵr, we obtain the effective densities of states Nc(T), Nv(T), intrinsic carrier density ni(T), and Wannier–Mott exciton binding energy Eb & Bohr radius aB*:

n_i(T) = \sqrt{N_{\mathrm{c}} N_{\mathrm{v}}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{g}}}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right), \qquad \mu^*_{\mathrm{ex}} = \frac{m^*_{\mathrm{e}}\,m^*_{\mathrm{h}}}{m^*_{\mathrm{e}} + m^*_{\mathrm{h}}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{b}}^{\mathrm{3D}} = 13.606\,\frac{\mu^*_{\mathrm{ex}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}^2}\;\mathrm{eV}, \qquad a_{\mathrm{B}}^* = a_0\,\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu^*_{\mathrm{ex}}}
(6.4)

6.3 Carrier Mobility (μe, μh), Multi-Channel Scattering & Diffusion

In the relaxation-time approximation of the Boltzmann Transport Equation, scattering rates from acoustic phonons (ADP), polar optical phonons (POP), and ionized impurities (IMP) add via Matthiessen's Rule, and mobility connects directly to carrier diffusivity via the Einstein relation:

\frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{ADP}}} + \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{POP}}} + \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{IMP}}}, \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{e\,\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}{m^*_{\mathrm{Drude}}}, \qquad D_c = \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{tot}}\,k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{e}
(6.5)

1. Acoustic Deformation Potential (Takagi 2D & Bardeen–Shockley 3D): Longitudinal acoustic strain ϵ shifts band edges by ΔEedge = E1ϵ. Using in-plane stiffness C2D = (1/S0)(∂2E/∂ϵ2) (N/m) or bulk elastic constant C3D = (1/Ω0)(∂2E/∂ϵ2) (GPa):

\mu_{\mathrm{ADP,2D}} = \frac{e\hbar^3 C_{\mathrm{2D}}}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,m^*_\alpha\,m^*_{\mathrm{d}}\,E_1^2}, \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{ADP,3D}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,e\hbar^4 C_{\mathrm{3D}}}{3\,(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^{3/2}\,m^*_\alpha\,(m^*_{\mathrm{d}})^{3/2}\,E_1^2}
(6.6)

2. Fröhlich Polar Optical Phonon (POP) & 3. Brooks–Herring Ionized Impurity (IMP): In polar crystals (ϵ0 > ϵ∞), LO phonons of energy ℏωLO couple to carriers through the dimensionless Fröhlich constant αF, while screened ionized impurities of density Ni dominate low-temperature transport (γBH = 24m*kBT/ℏ2βs2):

\alpha_{\mathrm{F}} = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar}\!\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon_\infty} - \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\right)\!\sqrt{\frac{m^*}{2\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{POP}} \approx \frac{e^{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}/k_{\mathrm{B}}T} - 1}{2\alpha_{\mathrm{F}}\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}}, \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{IMP}} \propto \frac{\varepsilon_0^2\,(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^{3/2}}{N_i\sqrt{m^*}\left[\ln(1+\gamma_{\mathrm{BH}}) - \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{BH}}}{1+\gamma_{\mathrm{BH}}}\right]}
(6.7)

6.4 Drude Effective Mass (m*Drude) & Drude Relaxation Time (τe, τh)

When a semiconductor is doped to electron density n or hole density p (or in a metal at EF), free carriers oscillate collectively at the Drude plasma frequency ωp and generate an intraband optical conductivity σDrude(ω) and dielectric tail ϵDrude(ω):

\omega_{\mathrm{p},c}^2(\mu_c, T) = \frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega}\sum_{n,\mathbf{k}} g_{\mathrm{s}}\,w_{\mathbf{k}}\,v_{n\mathbf{k}}^2\!\left(-\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial E}\right), \qquad m^*_{\mathrm{Drude},c}(n_c, T) = \frac{n_c\,e^2}{\varepsilon_0\,\omega_{\mathrm{p},c}^2}
(6.8)
For non-parabolic Kane bands at degenerate Fermi energy EF, m*Drude(EF) = m*0(1 + 2αKEF)—the Drude mass increases monotonically with doping.
\tau_c = \frac{\hbar}{\gamma_{\mathrm{D},c}} = \frac{\sigma_{0,c}\,m^*_{\mathrm{Drude},c}}{n_c\,e^2}, \qquad \varepsilon^{\mathrm{Drude}}(\omega) = \varepsilon_\infty - \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{p}}^2}{\omega(\omega + i\gamma_{\mathrm{D}})}, \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{Drude}}(\omega) = \frac{n e^2 \tau / m^*_{\mathrm{Drude}}}{1 - i\omega\tau}
(6.9)
Drude relaxation time τ (fs) maps directly onto the optical damping rate γD (eV) via τ[fs] = 0.65821 / γD[eV] and controls the carrier mean free path ℓ = vrmsτ.
HANDS-ON PRACTICE IN DATA ANALYSIS
🧪 Compute Band/DOS Effective Mass, Mobility & Drude τ on Real CASTEP Jobs
  1. Open Data Analysis → 🚀 m* & Drude with a semiconductor job (e.g., 2D Janus J1+4, Eg = 0.987 eV at K).
  2. Inspect the Conduction Band Edge (CBM) and Valence Band Edge (VBM) parabolic/Kane fits along K → Γ and K → M (m*e = 0.648 m0, m*h = 0.904 m0, R2 = 0.985–0.998).
  3. Compare DOS Mass (Band) vs. DOS Mass (DFT DOS), toggle POP & IMP scattering, sweep Drude m*(n,p) & ℏωp or Drude ϵ(ω) & σ1(ω), and click ⚡ e−/h+ Drude → Optical to inject your computed ℏωp and γD straight into the Optical tab!

dft_lectures.subtitle: From dipole momentum matrix elements in CASTEP *.ome_bin to complex dielectric tensor ϵ(ω), f-sum rule, polarization anisotropy, absorption α(ω), EELS, and Tauc gaps.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: optical properties dielectric function epsilon1 epsilon2 kramers kronig f-sum rule ome_bin momentum matrix dipole polarized unpolarized polycrystalline scissors levine allan absorption refractive index reflectivity eels loss function tauc plot gw bse exciton
objectives: Derive the interband imaginary dielectric tensor ϵ2(ω) from Fermi's Golden Rule and CASTEP *.ome_bin momentum matrix elements.
Apply the Kramers–Kronig causal relation, optical f-sum rule, Levine–Allan scissors shift, and intraband Drude term.
Distinguish Polarized, Unpolarized (normal to incidence q), and Polycrystalline (isotropic trace) tensor projections.
Convert ϵ<sub>1</sub>(ω), ϵ<sub>2</sub>(ω) into refractive index n/k, absorption α(ω), reflectivity R(ω), EELS L(ω), optical conductivity σ<sub>1</sub>(ω), and Tauc optical gap.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
7.1 Complex Dielectric Tensor & Interband Transitions (*.ome_bin)

When light of photon energy ℏω illuminates a crystal, vertical interband transitions promote electrons from occupied valence bands v to unoccupied conduction bands c at virtually unchanged wavevector k (qphoton ≈ 0). Within the independent-particle dipole approximation (IPA / Fermi's Golden Rule), the imaginary part of the symmetrized 3×3 dielectric tensor ϵ2,αβ(ω) is built directly from the optical momentum matrix elements pcvk} = ⟨ψck}|p|ψvk}⟩ stored in CASTEP binary *.ome_bin files:

\varepsilon_{2,\alpha\beta}(\omega) = \frac{4\pi^2 e^2}{\Omega m_0^2 \omega^2}\sum_{v,c,\mathbf{k}} g_{\mathrm{s}}\,w_{\mathbf{k}}\,(f_{v\mathbf{k}} - f_{c\mathbf{k}})\allowbreak\,\langle \psi_{c\mathbf{k}}|\hat{p}_\alpha|\psi_{v\mathbf{k}}\rangle\allowbreak\langle \psi_{v\mathbf{k}}|\hat{p}_\beta|\psi_{c\mathbf{k}}\rangle\allowbreak\,\delta(E_{c\mathbf{k}} - E_{v\mathbf{k}} - \hbar\omega)
(7.1)
A rigid Levine–Allan scissors shift Δsc corrects semilocal PBE gap underestimation (Ec − Ev → Ec − Ev + Δsc) while renormalizing matrix elements by (Ecv + Δsc)/Ecv to preserve the optical f-sum rule.

7.2 Causality, Kramers–Kronig Transform & Optical f-Sum Rule

Because electromagnetic polarization cannot precede the incident field (causality), the real dispersive part ϵ1,αβ(ω) follows uniquely from ϵ2,αβ(ω) via the Cauchy principal-value Kramers–Kronig transform, while total oscillator strength satisfies the Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn f-sum rule:

\varepsilon_{1,\alpha\beta}(\omega) = \delta_{\alpha\beta} + \frac{2}{\pi}\,\mathcal{P}\!\int_0^\infty \frac{\omega'\,\varepsilon_{2,\alpha\beta}(\omega')}{\omega'^2 - \omega^2}\,\mathrm{d}\omega', \qquad \int_0^\infty \omega\,\varepsilon_2(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\omega = \frac{\pi}{2}\,\omega_{\mathrm{p,val}}^2
(7.2)
Evaluating at ω = 0 yields the electronic static dielectric constant ϵ1(0) = ϵ∞ and static refractive index n(0) = √ϵ1(0). Sufficient unoccupied bands (optics_nbands) must be included so the f-sum rule converges.

7.3 Polarization Geometries (Crystal Anisotropy)

In anisotropic materials (especially 2D layered crystals where in-plane ϵxx = ϵyy differs dramatically from out-of-plane ϵzz), the scalar response ϵ(ω) depends on how light propagates relative to the crystal axes:

Calculation ModePhysical GeometryTensor Projection Formula
PolarizedLinearly polarized electric field along unit vector eϵpol(ω) = eT · ϵ(ω) · e
UnpolarizedRandomly polarized beam propagating along incidence q (E ⊥ q)ϵunpol(ω) = ½[Tr(ϵ) − qT · ϵ · q]
PolycrystallinePowder / randomly oriented grains (isotropic average)ϵpoly(ω) = ⅓(ϵxx + ϵyy + ϵzz)

7.4 Derived Optical Functions, Optical Conductivity & Tauc Optical Gap

From the complex dielectric function ϵ(ω) = ϵ1(ω) + iϵ2(ω) = (n + ik)2, every measurable optical spectrum follows analytically:

n(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\sqrt{\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2} + \varepsilon_1\right]^{1/2}, \qquad k(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\sqrt{\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2} - \varepsilon_1\right]^{1/2}
(7.3)
\alpha(\omega) = \frac{2\omega\,k(\omega)}{c}, \qquad R(\omega) = \frac{(n - 1)^2 + k^2}{(n + 1)^2 + k^2}, \qquad L(\omega) = \frac{\varepsilon_2}{\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2}, \qquad \sigma_1(\omega) = \varepsilon_0\omega\varepsilon_2(\omega)
(7.4)
Peaks in the Electron Energy Loss Function L(ω) = Im(−1/ϵ) mark collective bulk plasmon resonances (ℏωp). Note: Materials Studio CASTEP plots α = 2k/λ whereas SI optics textbooks use 4πk/λ—both conventions are selectable in our Optical More... menu.
(\alpha\,\hbar\omega)^{1/r} = A\left(\hbar\omega - E_{\mathrm{g}}^{\mathrm{opt}}\right), \qquad r = \frac{1}{2}\;(\text{direct allowed}), \quad r = 2\;(\text{indirect allowed})
(7.5)
Tauc Relation: Extrapolating the linear absorption onset of (αℏω)2 (direct) or (αℏω)1/2 (indirect) to zero gives the optical band gap Egopt.
💡 Physical Insight — When Independent-Particle DFT Optics Needs GW + BSE
Standard DFT optical spectra (Eq. 7.1) neglect electron–hole Coulomb attraction (excitons). In 3D bulk covalent semiconductors with large dielectric screening (ϵr > 10), IPA + Scissors matches experiment very well. In atomically thin 2D monolayers (MoS2, WS2, Janus TMDCs) where reduced screening creates large exciton binding energies (Eb = 0.3–0.8 eV), the optical gap satisfies Egopt = EgQP − Eb, requiring many-body GW + Bethe–Salpeter Equation (BSE) for exact excitonic peak positions.
HANDS-ON PRACTICE IN DATA ANALYSIS
🧪 Explore Full 3×3 Optical Tensor, Anisotropy & Tauc Fit

dft_lectures.subtitle: Visualizing real-space bond formation, interfacial electron accumulation/depletion, integrated charge transfer ΔQ(z), dipole-corrected work functions, Bader QTAIM, and ELF bonding topology.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: charge density difference chdiff charg_frm deformation density planar average integrated charge transfer deltaQ work function dipole correction elf electron localization function bader qtaim isosurface
objectives: Distinguish deformation density (*.chdiff) from interfacial/adsorption differential density (ρ<sub>AB</sub> − ρ<sub>A</sub> − ρ<sub>B</sub>).
Integrate 3D Δρ(x,y,z) into 1D planar-averaged Δρ(z) and cumulative electron transfer ΔQ(z).
Compute work functions Φ and interface dipole shifts ΔΦ via the Helmholtz equation and Neugebauer–Scheffler dipole correction.
Interpret Electron Localization Function (ELF) topology and compare Mulliken, Hirshfeld, and Bader QTAIM atomic charges.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
8.1 Two Physical Definitions of Charge Density Difference (Δρ)

Total valence electron density ρ(r) is dominated by nearly spherical core-adjacent shells, masking subtle chemical bonding rearrangements. Subtracting a well-defined reference isolates exact electron redistribution (yellow: accumulation +Δρ, cyan: depletion −Δρ):

\textbf{Deformation Density:}\quad \Delta\rho_{\mathrm{def}}(\mathbf{r}) = \rho_{\mathrm{SCF}}(\mathbf{r}) - \sum_I \rho_I^{\mathrm{free\ atom}}(\mathbf{r})
(8.1)
Shows how neutral isolated atoms deform upon crystal bond formation—positive accumulation lobes along bond midpoints directly expose covalent shared electron pairs.
\textbf{Interfacial / Adsorption Density:}\quad \Delta\rho_{\mathrm{ads}}(\mathbf{r}) = \rho_{\mathrm{AB}}(\mathbf{r}) - \rho_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathbf{r}) - \rho_{\mathrm{B}}(\mathbf{r})
(8.2)
Must be computed on the exact same FFT grid, supercell dimensions, and fixed atomic coordinates for the combined system (AB) and isolated fragments (A = slab, B = adsorbate or second 2D layer).

8.2 1D Planar-Averaged Δρ(z) & Integrated Charge Transfer ΔQ(z)

For 2D surfaces, van der Waals heterojunctions (e.g., WS2/MoSe2), and adsorbed catalysts, integrating Δρ(x,y,z) across the in-plane unit cell area Sab collapses 3D clouds into a quantitative 1D charge-transfer curve along surface normal z:

\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{1D}}(z) = \iint_{S_{ab}} \Delta\rho(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y, \qquad \Delta Q(z) = \int_0^z \Delta\rho_{\mathrm{1D}}(z')\,\mathrm{d}z'
(8.3)
Charge conservation guarantees ΔQ(c) = 0 across the full cell. The extremum max |ΔQ(z)| at the interfacial zero-crossing plane gives the exact number of electrons transferred from donor to acceptor layer.

8.3 Work Function (Φ), Dipole Correction & Electron Localization Function (ELF)

The work function Φ is the minimum energy to remove an electron from EF into the flat vacuum electrostatic potential Vvac. Interfacial charge transfer induces a surface dipole Δμz that shifts Φ via the Helmholtz equation. In asymmetric slabs (Janus monolayers or single-sided adsorption), a sawtooth Neugebauer–Scheffler dipole correction eliminates artificial periodic electric fields across the vacuum:

\Phi = V_{\mathrm{vac}} - E_{\mathrm{F}}, \qquad \Delta\Phi = -\frac{e}{\varepsilon_0}\Delta\mu_z = -\frac{e}{\varepsilon_0 S_{ab}}\int z\,\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{1D}}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z
(8.4)

To classify local electron pairing without a promolecule reference, Becke and Edgecombe formulated the dimensionless Electron Localization Function (ELF) ∈ [0, 1] comparing the excess Pauli kinetic energy density D(r) to a uniform electron gas Dh(r) = (3/10)(3π2)2/3n5/3:

\mathrm{ELF}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{1 + \left[D(\mathbf{r}) / D_{\mathrm{h}}(\mathbf{r})\right]^2}, \qquad D(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left|\nabla\phi_i\right|^2 - \frac{1}{8}\frac{|\nabla n|^2}{n}
(8.5)
ELF = 1.0: perfect spin-paired localization (covalent bonds, lone pairs); ELF ≈ 0.5: homogeneous electron gas (metallic bonding); ELF → 0: low-density closed-shell ionic regions.

8.4 Comparing Atomic Charge Partitioning Schemes

Because "atomic charge" inside a solid is not a unique quantum observable, DFT employs four complementary partitioning schemes—including Bader's Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM), which divides space strictly along zero-flux density surfaces ∇ρ(r) · n = 0:

MethodPartitioning PrincipleBasis DependenceBest Use & Caveats
Mulliken (LCAO)Projects plane waves onto atomic orbitals; splits overlap equallyModerate (sensitive to spilling)Gives Bond Overlap Population & orbital s/p/d breakdown in CASTEP
HirshfeldReal-space stockholder weights wI = ρIfree / ∑ρJfreeNone (density-only)Smooth trends & TS vdW volumes; magnitudes tend to be small (∼0.3× formal)
Bader (QTAIM)Topological zero-flux basins (∇ρ · n = 0)None (fine FFT grid)Quantitative ionic/adsorption charge transfer (requires core + valence density)
Born Effective Charge Z*Dynamic polarization response Z*αβ = Ω∂Pα/∂uβNone (DFPT)Ferroelectrics (BaTiO3), LO–TO phonon splitting, dynamical covalency

  2. Adjust Plane ((010), (100), (001)), slide Pos through atomic layers, tune Iso (e/Å3), and read quantitative Max |ΔQ(z)| in the 1D Planar Profile panel.
  3. Click 🧱 3D Isosurface to project volumetric yellow/cyan Δρ clouds directly inside the interactive 3D VESTA viewer!

dft_lectures.subtitle: From collinear LSDA, Stoner ferromagnetism, and Heisenberg exchange Jij to non-collinear SOC, overlap bond populations, and orbital-resolved 5×5 d-orbital spin matrices.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: spin polarized magnetism lsda stoner heisenberg exchange curie temperature non-collinear soc spin orbit coupling mae ferromagnetic fm antiferromagnetic afm ferrimagnetic fim mulliken hirshfeld bond population spin matrix crystal field t2g eg d-orbital
objectives: Formulate collinear spin-polarized DFT (n↑, n↓), Stoner ferromagnetism, and non-collinear vector magnetization with Spin–Orbit Coupling (SOC).
Differentiate Ferromagnetic (FM), Antiferromagnetic (AFM), and Ferrimagnetic (FiM) states and map DFT energies onto the Heisenberg model Jij & Curie temperature TC.
Contrast Mulliken LCAO atomic/bond populations with Hirshfeld stockholder charges.
Interpret the 5×5 d-orbital Spin Matrix via crystal-field splitting (t2g vs. eg) and Goodenough–Kanamori superexchange.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
9.1 Collinear Spin-Polarized DFT, Stoner Criterion & Non-Collinear SOC

In open-shell transition metals, defects, and radicals, spin-up (↑, α) and spin-down (↓, β) electrons experience distinct exchange potentials because Pauli exchange acts solely between parallel spins. Spin-polarized DFT splits total density and magnetization density into two coupled channels:

n(\mathbf{r}) = n_\uparrow(\mathbf{r}) + n_\downarrow(\mathbf{r}), \qquad m(\mathbf{r}) = n_\uparrow(\mathbf{r}) - n_\downarrow(\mathbf{r}), \qquad M_{\mathrm{net}} = \mu_{\mathrm{B}}\int m(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}
(9.1)
Comparing net moment Mnet = ∑μI against absolute moment Mabs = ∑|μI| identifies the magnetic phase: FM (|Mnet| ≈ Mabs), AFM (Mnet ≈ 0, Mabs > 0), or FiM (0 < |Mnet| < Mabs). In itinerant metals, spontaneous spin splitting occurs when the Stoner Criterion IStoner · g(EF) > 1 is met.

Mapping total energies of FM and AFM spin configurations onto the Heisenberg Spin Hamiltonian determines inter-site magnetic exchange constants Jij and the mean-field Curie/Néel ordering temperature TC, while relativistic Spin–Orbit Coupling (SOC) (λSOC L·S) with 2-component Pauli spinors yields the Magnetic Anisotropy Energy (MAE):

\hat{H}_{\mathrm{spin}} = -\sum_{i < j} J_{ij}\,\mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j, \qquad T_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{MF}} = \frac{2 z J\,S(S+1)}{3 k_{\mathrm{B}}}, \qquad \mathrm{MAE} = E_{\parallel} - E_{\perp}
(9.2)
Positive J > 0 favors ferromagnetism; negative J < 0 favors antiferromagnetism (governed in oxides and cyanides like KCoHCF by the Goodenough–Kanamori–Anderson superexchange rules).

9.2 Mulliken Population, Overlap Bond Population & Hirshfeld Charges

Because plane waves span the entire unit cell, CASTEP projects converged Bloch states onto a localized atomic-orbital basis {χμ} (Segall–Pickard formalism) to compute the density matrix P and overlap matrix S:

q_I^{\mathrm{Mulliken}} = Z_I^{\mathrm{val}} - \sum_{\mu \in I}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S})_{\mu\mu}, \qquad P_{IJ}^{\mathrm{bond}} = 2\sum_{\mu\in I,\,\nu\in J} P_{\mu\nu}\,S_{\nu\mu}
(9.3)
Mulliken Bond Population PIJ: large positive values (+0.5 to +1.9, e.g., C≡N or Si–N) indicate strong covalent bonding; values near 0 indicate ionic character; negative values denote antibonding repulsion.

Hirshfeld ("Stockholder") Population Analysis partitions real-space density directly using promolecule atomic weights, making Hirshfeld charges basis-set-independent:

w_I(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\rho_I^{\mathrm{free}}(\mathbf{r})}{\sum_J \rho_J^{\mathrm{free}}(\mathbf{r})}, \qquad q_I^{\mathrm{Hirsh}} = Z_I^{\mathrm{val}} - \int w_I(\mathbf{r})\,\rho_{\mathrm{SCF}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}
(9.4)

9.3 Orbital-Resolved Spin Density Matrix & Crystal-Field Splitting

Decomposing atomic spin moments μI = ∑l,m (nI,lm↑ − nI,lm↓) μB across individual magnetic quantum numbers—px, py, pz and the five d-orbitals (dz2, dzy, dzx, dx2−y2, dxy)—constructs the Orbital-Resolved Spin Matrix:

S_{m,m'}^{(I,l)} = \delta_{mm'}\left(n_{I,lm}^\uparrow - n_{I,lm}^\downarrow\right)\mu_{\mathrm{B}}, \qquad \mathrm{Tr}\!\left[\mathbf{S}^{(I,l)}\right] = \mu_{I,l}
(9.5)
HANDS-ON PRACTICE IN DATA ANALYSIS
🧪 Inspect Orbital-Resolved Spin Matrices, Charges & 3D Spin Arrows
  1. Open Data Analysis → 🧲 Mulliken & Spin on a spin-polarized job (e.g., KCoHCF+K CASTEP Energy).
  2. Use the Orbital-Resolved Spin Matrix element pills (All Elements Grid, Co, Fe, N, C, K) to inspect the exact 5×5 d-orbital or 3×3 p-orbital spin heatmap and orbital share breakdown.
  3. Scroll down to the Mulliken Charts Toolbar to compare Atomic Magnetic Moment (μB), Mulliken vs. Hirshfeld Charge, and Bond Population vs. Bond Length, or click 🧲 3D Spin Arrows to overlay red (↑) / blue (↓) magnetic vectors onto the crystal structure.

dft_lectures.title: Lecture 10: Exchange Splitting, Spin Polarization, Half-Metallicity & Stoner Itinerant Magnetism
dft_lectures.subtitle: Quantifying spin-resolved DOS asymmetry, Fermi-level spin polarization P(EF), exchange splitting Δex, the Stoner criterion I·D(EF) > 1, and electric-field / doping-induced spontaneous ferromagnetism.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: exchange splitting delta_ex spin polarization P(EF) half metal half-metallicity stoner model stoner criterion stoner parameter I itinerant ferromagnetism paramagnetic susceptibility enhancement rigid band van hove singularity doping electric field induced magnetism pdos
objectives: Compute the spin-resolved total density of states D(E), Fermi-level spin asymmetry ΔD(EF), spin polarization P(EF), and integrated total magnetic moment Mtot from first-principles DOS/PDOS.
Extract the exchange splitting energy Δex from majority (↑) and minority (↓) PDOS peaks near EF and cross-check it with rigid-band cross-correlation and band-center shifts.
Derive the Stoner Landau total-energy expansion E(m), the Stoner criterion I·D(EF) > 1, and the Stoner-enhanced Pauli susceptibility χ/χ0.
Determine the effective Stoner exchange parameter I = Δex / Mtot directly from DFT and predict electric-field or carrier-doping-induced magnetic phase transitions in 2D materials.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
10.1 Spin-Resolved Density of States & Spin Polarization at EF

In a collinear spin-polarized DFT calculation, the Kohn–Sham eigenstates separate into independent majority-spin (↑, α) and minority-spin (↓, β) channels. Summing both spin channels yields the total density of states (TDOS) D(E), while their difference at the Fermi energy EF defines the Fermi-level spin asymmetry ΔD(EF):

D(E) = D_\uparrow(E) + D_\downarrow(E), \qquad \Delta D(E_{\mathrm{F}}) = D_\uparrow(E_{\mathrm{F}}) - D_\downarrow(E_{\mathrm{F}})
(10.1)
Here D↑(E) and D↓(E) are normalized per formula unit (states eV−1 f.u.−1) by dividing the unit-cell DOS by the number of formula units Z per simulation cell.

The spin polarization at the Fermi energy, P(EF), quantifies the spin-filtering efficiency of conduction carriers in spintronic junctions (such as magnetic tunnel junctions governed by Jullière's magnetoresistance formula) and is expressed as a percentage:

P(E_{\mathrm{F}}) = \frac{D_\uparrow(E_{\mathrm{F}}) - D_\downarrow(E_{\mathrm{F}})}{D_\uparrow(E_{\mathrm{F}}) + D_\downarrow(E_{\mathrm{F}})} \times 100\% = \frac{\Delta D(E_{\mathrm{F}})}{D(E_{\mathrm{F}})} \times 100\%
(10.2)

Integrating the spin-density difference across all occupied electronic states up to the Fermi level yields the total magnetic moment per formula unit Mtot (in units of Bohr magnetons μB/f.u.):

M_{\mathrm{tot}} = \mu_{\mathrm{B}} \int_{-\infty}^{E_{\mathrm{F}}} \left[D_\uparrow(E) - D_\downarrow(E)\right]\mathrm{d}E
(10.3)
For accurate numerical integration, the lower bound must span all occupied valence states below EF (not merely a narrow plotting window), and the result should agree closely with CASTEP's SCF 2*Integrated Spin Density / Z.
Electronic / Magnetic PhaseD↑(EF) & D↓(EF)|P(EF)|Mtot (μB/f.u.)Spintronic Significance
Non-Magnetic / Paramagnetic MetalD↑ = D↓ > 00%0Spin-degenerate bands; susceptible to Stoner transition if I·D(EF) → 1
Itinerant Ferromagnetic MetalD↑ ≠ D↓, both > 00% < |P| < 100%Non-integerConventional ferromagnets (bcc Fe, hcp Co, fcc Ni); partial spin filtering
Half-Metallic Ferromagnet (HMF)One channel metallic, one gapped100%Exact integerIdeal spin injector (Heusler alloys, CrO2, doped 2D layers); quantified by spin-flip gap EHM
Ferromagnetic SemiconductorD↑ = D↓ = 0 (both gapped)GappedInteger > 0Spin-split VBM/CBM edges; enables optical spin selectivity & dilute magnetic semiconductors

10.2 Exchange Splitting Energies (Δex) & Rigid-Band Picture

The intra-atomic Pauli exchange interaction lowers the potential energy of electrons with parallel spins relative to antiparallel spins, lifting spin degeneracy and shifting majority-spin (↑) states downward relative to minority-spin (↓) states. Within first-principles electronic structure analysis, the exchange splitting energy Δex is evaluated directly from the energy separation between the dominant corresponding spin-up and spin-down projected density of states (PDOS) peaks near the Fermi level:

\Delta_{\mathrm{ex}} = \left| E_{\mathrm{peak},\downarrow} - E_{\mathrm{peak},\uparrow} \right|
(10.4)
When orbital hybridization broadens the PDOS into multi-peak manifolds, Δex from dominant peak separation should be cross-checked against (i) the nearest-to-EF prominent peak pair, (ii) the rigid-band cross-correlation shift maximizing ∫D↑(E)D↓(E+δ) dE, and (iii) the first-moment band-center difference |Ē↓ − Ē↑|.

10.3 The Stoner Model of Itinerant Magnetism & the Stoner Criterion

Unlike localized Heisenberg moments on insulating transition-metal ions, itinerant magnetism in metals, doped semiconductors, and gated 2D sheets arises from a delicate competition between kinetic energy and exchange energy. Transferring δn = m/2 electrons per formula unit from spin-down into spin-up states near EF raises their band kinetic energy by ΔEkin = ½ m2 / D(EF) (Pauli exclusion penalty), while the intra-atomic Coulomb exchange interaction lowers the energy by ΔEex = −½ I m2. Expanding the total energy as a Landau functional of the magnetic moment m gives:

E(m) = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{D(E_{\mathrm{F}})} - I\right] m^2 + \mathcal{O}(m^4)
(10.5)
Here D(EF) is the non-magnetic density of states at the Fermi level per formula unit (or spin-averaged DOS, states eV−1 f.u.−1), and I is the Stoner exchange parameter (eV), quantifying the intra-atomic electron–electron Coulomb exchange interaction.

The non-magnetic state (m = 0) becomes thermodynamically unstable against spontaneous ferromagnetic spin splitting whenever the quadratic curvature turns negative, yielding the celebrated Stoner Criterion and the Stoner-enhanced Pauli spin susceptibility χ:

I \cdot D(E_{\mathrm{F}}) > 1 \quad (\text{Spontaneous FM}), \qquad \chi = \frac{\chi_0}{1 - I \cdot D(E_{\mathrm{F}})}
(10.6)
📘 Definition — Thermodynamic Regimes of the Stoner Criterion
  • When I · D(EF) < 1: The quadratic coefficient is positive, forming a single-well parabola centered at m = 0; the paramagnetic / non-magnetic state is stable. When I · D(EF) approaches 1 from below (e.g., Pd with I·D ≈ 0.8), spin fluctuations produce massive Stoner enhancement χ/χ0 = [1 − I·D(EF)]−1 ≫ 1.
  • When I · D(EF) > 1: The quadratic curvature turns negative, creating a symmetric double-well Landau potential with equilibrium minima at m = ±Mtot ≠ 0; spontaneous itinerant ferromagnetism is thermodynamically favored!

10.4 First-Principles Estimation of the Stoner Exchange Parameter (I)

Within rigid-band Stoner theory (Gunnarsson 1976; Janak 1977), shifting the majority and minority spin bands apart by the exchange splitting Δex is linearly proportional to the self-consistent magnetization Mtot:

\Delta_{\mathrm{ex}} = I \cdot M_{\mathrm{tot}} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad I = \frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{ex}}}{M_{\mathrm{tot}}}
(10.7)
With Δex in eV and Mtot in μB/f.u., the extracted effective Stoner parameter I has units of eV. Typical values span 0.6–1.0 eV for 3d/4d transition metals and 1.0–1.6 eV for localized 2p/3p states.

10.5 Electric-Field & Doping-Induced Spontaneous Magnetism in 2D Materials

Many pristine 2D semiconductors—such as monolayer GaSe, InSe, and Janus transition-metal dichalcogenides—are non-magnetic in their neutral ground state because EF lies inside the band gap (D(EF) = 0). However, inverted "Mexican-hat" valence bands and saddle-point Van Hove singularities (VHS) produce ultra-sharp peaks in D(E) right near the band edges. Applying a perpendicular electric field or electrostatic hole/electron doping (Δn) shifts EF directly into this high-DOS manifold, driving I·D(EF) > 1 and switching on spontaneous, reversible Stoner ferromagnetism and half-metallicity (Cao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 2015).

💡 Physical Insight — Crucial DFT Subtlety: Non-Magnetic vs. Post-Splitting D(E_F)

Always check which density of states is inserted into I·D(EF)! In a strongly spin-split ferromagnet or half-metal, once spontaneous spin splitting opens up (Δex > 0), the high-DOS peak splits apart and shifts away from EF, reducing the post-splitting spin-polarized D(EF). To test the onset of the Stoner instability rigorously, evaluate DNM(EF) either from a separate non-magnetic calculation (spin_polarized: false) or from the Rigid-Band Unsplit DOS DNM*(EF) automatically reconstructed inside our live 🧭 Stoner analyzer!
